name: Domestic blue-box trunk seizure
preconditions: answer supervision returned by the far CO
steps: Dial a long-distance number you legitimately reach.
After answer supervision, play 2600 Hz into the audio path for ~700 ms (switch-dependent: 4ESS >=400 ms).
The originating tandem reads far-end on-hook and drops the trunk to a wink/idle while your local loop stays up.
MF-pulse KP + destination digits + ST as if you were an originating tandem.
The tandem routes your new call.
vulnerability_window: Died as trunks migrated SF/MF -> CCIS/SS7. Impractical on major US routes by ~1990; straggler independents into the mid-1990s.
retirement_cause: Out-of-band signaling (CCIS No.6, then SS7): a 2600 Hz tone in the voice path is now just audio.

name: AUTOVON precedence preemption
preconditions: line originating on an AUTOVON subscriber station (silver-box or AUTOVON-capable Class-A phone)
shared AUTOVON trunk with lower-precedence traffic to preempt
authorization to use the requested precedence level (military rank / role determined dial-plan authorization on Class-A stations)
steps: Off-hook the AUTOVON station; hear AUTOVON dial tone.
Optionally press ONE precedence key BEFORE dialing: A=Flash Override, B=Flash, C=Immediate, D=Priority. No key = Routine.
Dial the 3-digit AUTOVON theater prefix + 7-digit off-net address (or a fully-off-net 800/civilian-gateway number).

If the trunks between the origin and destination are congested, the switch preempts the LOWEST-precedence call currently on a trunk that would otherwise carry your call — Flash Override displaces everyone up to and including three-star Flash traffic.
The preempted party hears a preemption tone and their call is dropped.
vulnerability_window: Effective on AUTOVON (1966 through DoD's shift to DSN, ~1990). DSN retained the precedence concept but the fourth-column DTMF-key mechanism was superseded by ISDN precedence and, later, IP-based Assured Services (AS-SIP RPH headers, ETS).
retirement_cause: AUTOVON decommissioned ~1990 in favor of DSN; A/B/C/D keys were removed from most successor phones. Modern MLPP uses ISDN or SIP RPH.

name: Meridian / SL-1 DISA abuse via craft-interface access
preconditions: TTY/modem access to the target SL-1 / Meridian 1 SDI or MSDL port
Default admin login accepted (ADMIN1/0000, ADMIN2/0000, PWD1/0000, MAINT/0000) OR a captured admin credential
Package 26 (DISA) licensed on the switch (verifiable via LD 22 PRT PKG)
steps: Scan an unpublished DID range with a war-dialer; identify a modem answering with an SL-1 login prompt (see 'Enter Login:' or attention-getting banner).
Log in with era-typical defaults (ADMIN1/0000 etc.). LD 22, then PRT PKG — confirm DISA (26) and check for MCT (107).
LD 15 — enable DISA on the customer: set DISA=YES, define the DISA DN, set required auth-code length (often 4-6 digits).
LD 88 — add a fresh authorization code with NEW; pick a CODE, set COS = permissive, set NCOS pointing to an FRL-0 network CoS.
LD 91 — verify (or set) NCOS with FRL 0 so the code can traverse international routes.
LD 16 — verify (or add) a route to the target destination with liberal FRL and no digit stripping.
LD 40 — optionally disable or redirect CDR so the fraudulent call doesn't land in the customer's monthly detail report.
END out of each overlay to commit. From any outside line, dial the DISA DN, hear second dial tone, enter the auth code, then dial internationally as if from the enterprise.
Cleanup: LD 40 restore CDR, LD 88 OUT the added code (or leave it if the target isn't watching).
vulnerability_window: Effective 1985 through today on unpatched, default-credentialed Meridian / CS1000 systems. Modern deployments enforce credential rotation and CDR alerting, but abandoned or acquisition-orphaned PBXs (small hotels, warehouses, medical offices) remain vulnerable.
retirement_cause: Not retired — the SL-1 / Meridian / CS1000 family is still installed, though shrinking as Avaya and Cisco IP-PBX successors displace them.

name: Red-box a fortress phone at an ACTS prompt
preconditions: an ACTS-equipped Bell single-slot (fortress) payphone whose 1700+2200 Hz coin receiver is on the toll switch
steps: Dial a long-distance number from a fortress phone.
ACTS voice prompt: 'Please deposit X.'
Instead of coins, play the 1700+2200 Hz coin-tone bursts into the mouthpiece (quarter = five 33 ms bursts per GR-506-CORE).
ACTS credits the deposit and cuts the call through.
vulnerability_window: Worked ~1978 until ACTS single-slots were retrofitted/replaced 1996-2002.
retirement_cause: Local coin validation in smart payphones (Millennium/COCOT) and T1/robbed-bit trunks stripping in-band ACTS supervision.
